headline: No Rice, no Moore: the Chiefs need answers at Seattle
dek: Seattle is the assignment now: protect Mahomes without Rice and Moore, give Walker a real answer against a stubborn run front, and keep Smith-Njigba in view. Kickoff is October 25 at 7:20 p.m. Central on NBC. This is a pregame edition.
videoHook: The record is perfect. The lineup is not. Seattle is where the Chiefs have to make the next answer work.
theEdge: Our read: give Mahomes a quick answer before asking for a deep one. Make Seattle defend the width of the formation, then let Walker attack the space that creates. This is a pregame plan, not a prediction of the final score.

storyline.lede: Five wins buy belief. They do not fill tonight’s vacancies. Kansas City’s next step is to make the offense coherent with the players available, then let the defense play a full field.
body: This is why the Seattle trip is worth watching beyond the record. A good offense has answers that survive a changed lineup. The formation should explain the protection, the route spacing should explain the first read, and the checkdown should be part of the play rather than a rescue mission.

There is no result to grade yet. Judge the opening possessions by the quality of the decisions: clean operation, useful early-down gains and a quarterback who knows where the ball can go when the first look disappears. The scoreboard will supply the verdict later.

analysis.body: Walker ran for 128 yards and two touchdowns; Worthy caught seven passes for 73 yards. Those contributions point toward tonight's question: can the available weapons keep the offense on schedule when Seattle squeezes the run?

currentState.lede: Kansas City brings a 5-0 record to Lumen Field; Seattle is 3-3. The useful question is what works tonight. The official Friday report rules out Rashee Rice and Jaylon Moore, and Saturday brought roster reinforcements. Game-day inactives are still the final check, not something this preview assumes.

workOn.title: Set the protection before the noise
workOn.body: Give the replacement tackle help with alignment, a chip or a quick release when the matchup needs it. A tight end cannot be both a permanent extra blocker and an immediate outlet. Decide which job matters on each call.

workOn.title: Give the receiving rotation a job
workOn.body: Worthy can stretch a defender’s leverage. Armstrong can work a defined route. The underneath option needs to arrive on time. Do not ask every available receiver to impersonate Rice; build a progression the quarterback can finish.

workOn.title: Let the run set up the answer
workOn.body: Keep a pass available when Seattle commits numbers to Walker. If the front wins a run, the next call should attack what the defense showed rather than simply repeat the collision.

thinkAbout.title: Availability is not a snap count
thinkAbout.body: An activation or elevation makes a player available for selection. It does not promise a start, a workload or even an active jersey. Keep the roster transaction and the football projection separate.

thinkAbout.title: A clean possession has value
thinkAbout.body: A road offense can help its defense by avoiding a short field. The aggressive throw still belongs in the plan, but it needs protection and leverage, not just a desire to make a statement.

gamePlan.lede: Our suggested plan starts with manageable decisions: protect the edge, spread the underneath coverage and earn the shot play. The calls below are proposals, not claims about what Kansas City has already installed.
gamePlan.howTheyMatch: The Chiefs’ official Saturday preview sets the central matchup: Walker against a Seattle defense that has gone 35 straight games without allowing a 100-yard rusher. On the other side, it identifies Jaxon Smith-Njigba as the focal point of Seattle’s passing game. Winning either matchup requires more than one defender or one blocker doing his job.

keys.title: Move the launch point with purpose
keys.body: Seattle has gone 35 games without conceding a 100-yard rusher, according to the Chiefs' Saturday preview. Make that front defend width as well as the interior. A boot is useful only if the edge squeezes; if he stays home, Mahomes needs the short outlet. The animation below shows that read as an illustration, not a play already called.

keys.title: Know where Smith-Njigba is
keys.body: Smith-Njigba is Seattle's central receiving threat in the official matchup preview. Match the coverage to his alignment, carry the crossing route between zones and keep help over the top. Make the catch happen where the defense can rally, rather than donating an open runway.

keys.title: Make Seattle earn the field
keys.body: The official preview identifies Seattle's recent giveaways and protection trouble. Connected rush lanes can turn those vulnerabilities into difficult decisions, but a turnover is not owed to Kansas City. Win leverage, tackle the catch and make Seattle execute another down.

script: Open with inside zone and read how Seattle fits it.
Show the same backfield action, then give Mahomes a boot with an outlet.
Use mesh against man coverage; settle into space against zone.
Keep a running-back screen available against an aggressive rush.
Start with a two-high picture and rally to the underneath throw.
Change the pressure picture without abandoning the coverage responsibility.

xsandos.title: Make the front declare
xsandos.situation: Early downs, before choosing the next constraint
xsandos.why: Inside zone asks the blockers to work together and gives the runner a cut based on the fit. Use the response to choose the next call.
xsandos.coaching: Keep the combination blocks connected; press the track before cutting.

xsandos.title: Change the launch point
xsandos.situation: After a run look has drawn the edge inward
xsandos.why: A boot can move the quarterback away from the initial rush. It needs an outlet if the edge defender stays home.
xsandos.coaching: Sell the run action, then read the edge. Do not turn a covered outlet into a forced throw.

xsandos.title: Create a clean crossing window
xsandos.situation: Against man coverage, with a zone answer built in
xsandos.why: Crossing routes can separate through traffic. Against zone, the receivers need space to settle rather than running into the same window.
xsandos.coaching: Keep legal spacing through the cross and make the coverage declare.

xsandos.title: Make the rush travel
xsandos.situation: When the defense attacks the pocket
xsandos.why: A running-back screen invites the rush forward before sending the ball behind it. Timing matters more than surprise.
xsandos.coaching: Let the rush commit, release the blockers on time and secure the catch.

xsandos.title: Keep a lid on the shot
xsandos.situation: Early downs with two deep safeties
xsandos.why: Cover 2 puts a safety over each deep half while underneath defenders rally to the ball. The middle still needs an alert handoff.
xsandos.coaching: Disrupt releases without losing the flat; safeties stay deeper than the deepest threat.

xsandos.title: Change who is coming
xsandos.situation: A passing down where the coverage can support pressure
xsandos.why: A zone blitz sends an unexpected rusher and drops another defender into coverage. The exchange must leave a complete coverage structure.
xsandos.coaching: Identify the dropper and the vacated zone before the snap; rush with contain.

coaching.topic: Give every call a failure answer
coaching.detail: A covered first read should lead to a defined second decision. That is especially valuable when the protection has changed.
